tum

then, at that time

The plain word of classical prose. In a series tum also means “next” (see then, next).

Other words

  • tunc — then, at that very time

    also used · classical

    Lewis & Short: in classical prose tunc is emphatic (“just then”), and Cicero writes tum about thirty times as often; it becomes common only after Augustus.

  • eō tempore — at that time

    ablative of time · also used · classical · Liv. 6.38.12: eō tempore, quō prōmulgātum dē multā ejus trāditur (Lewis & Short s.v. tempus)

  • id temporis — at that time of day, at that hour

    the neuter id with a genitive, used as an adverb · also used · classical · Cic. Mil. 28 (Lewis & Short s.v. is); Traupman 88: at that time, ad id temporis; Traupman 394

    Like id aetātis (see age). Traupman’s ad id temporis would rather be “up to that time” (see until).

Examples

  • tunc maximē

    just thenTraupman 393
